Outcome: Depression cases (lower is better)

## Study A
Found: benefit
Claim: Among women supplemented with 800 IU vitamin D, those who remained vitamin D deficient before delivery had a significantly higher incidence of depression than those who reached insufficiency.
Sentence: "The incidence of depression in patients in vitamin D deficiency group following vitamin D supplementation was significantly higher than insufficiency group and reached statistical significance (P < 0.001)."
Measured as: incidence of prenatal depression
Population: Pregnant women diagnosed with vitamin D deficiency at 12-14 weeks of gestation, single tertiary hospital in Chengdu, China
Intervention: Vitamin D 800 IU daily from 14 weeks of gestation
Comparator: Women who achieved vitamin D insufficiency after supplementation versus those who remained deficient
Design: cohort study
Sample size: 1,365
baseline_vitamin_d_status: below_20_ng_ml

## Study B
Found: harm
Claim: Vitamin D level was significantly related to risk of depression (PHQ-9 above 5) six months after COVID-19 hospital admission; the direction is not stated in the abstract.
Sentence: "The variables that were significantly related to the risk of depression 6 months after admission for COVID-19 were frailty (p = 0.006 for pre-frail and p = 0.001 for frail), small-vessel vascular disease in imaging tests (p = 0.033), vitamin D level (p = 0.006), and taking antidepressants (p = 0.011)."
Measured as: risk of depression (PHQ-9 above 5)
Population: 72 patients admitted to a hospital in Spain for COVID-19, assessed at discharge and six months later
Intervention: Serum vitamin D level (measured, not administered)
Comparator: Lower versus higher vitamin D levels across participants
Design: cohort study
Sample size: 72
baseline_vitamin_d_status: not_reported
